events.title: Portuguese Oman
hints: In 1507 a fleet under Afonso de Albuquerque sacked the capital's coastal towns.
Great fortresses were built overlooking the harbour, and they controlled the entrance to the Gulf.
An imam of the Ya'ariba dynasty expelled the last Portuguese in 1650.
events.summary: Portugal captured the coastal towns in 1507 and held the port of Muscat, building forts such as Al Jalali and Al Mirani. Sultan bin Saif al-Ya'ruba took Muscat in 1650, ending the Portuguese presence.

events.title: British influence over Muscat
hints: A treaty in 1798 aimed to keep a French rival out of the Gulf and the Indian Ocean.
British officers advised the ruler, and the interior was treated as a separate territory.
A palace coup in 1970 replaced a ruler seen as isolationist, and Britain backed the change.
events.summary: From the 1798 treaty with the East India Company, Britain became the dominant outside power on the Omani coast, with advisers, loans and a military presence. In 1970, with British support, Sultan Qaboos overthrew his father, Said bin Taimur.

events.title: Dhofar rebellion and foreign backing
hints: A rebellion in the southern province began in 1962 against an isolationist ruler.
Britain and Iran sent forces and advisers, while the rebels received Soviet-bloc and South Yemeni support.
events.summary: A rebellion began in Dhofar in 1962 and grew into a Marxist-led insurgency backed by South Yemen and Soviet-bloc states. Britain provided officers, air support and SAS teams, and Iran sent troops, until the Sultan declared victory in December 1975, with fighting ending in 1976.
